newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Buba's Sievert says sees no immediate rate moves.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Sievert says sees no immediate rate moves.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Olaf Sievert said on Friday he ruled out a move in Germany's key rates over the next weeks but said it was not possible to predict interest rate moves over the next months.

"I don't think you can predict it over the next few months. But everybody knows that nothing will happen over the next few weeks," he told a bankers' conference in response to questions after a speech on European currency union and employment.
Sievert's remarks came just two days after Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing dashed hopes for an easing in Germany's key rates, which are already at historical lows.
Issing also said early Friday on German television that "under existing circumstances," there could be no rate cut in Germany but said he could not rule out rate cuts forever.

Sievert said the path of M3 money supply, the central bank's key policy guide, was not yet entirely clear, but he could not rule out that it would hit its four- to seven-percent target corridor this year.
"It's not sure yet how the money supply indicator will develop. It can't be ruled out that M3 will be on target," he said.
German M3 money supply growth slowed to 8.4 percent in September down from 8.7 percent in August, and the Bundesbank has insisted there is a trend towards an M3 slowdown.
Sievert, who also heads the state central bank for Saxony and Thuringia, added the German economy would benefit from a drop in long-term real interest rates, currently at around six percent.
"We would have to wish for lower long-term rates and the pre-conditions for that are not so bad," he said.
"We need lower real interest rates and judging by future inflation expectations, I would find that justified."
German inflation hovers around 1.5 percent, and analysts agree there are few reasons to expect an early upturn.
However, the Bundesbank member warned the link between short-term and long-term interest rates was weak, so that a cut at the short end may not fully filter through to the long end.

Sievert said long-term rates may be downwardly rigid because of concerns in financial markets that a future European single currency, scheduled to go into effect 1999, may not be as hard as the German mark, Europe's anchor currency.
In his earlier speech to the bankers' conference, Sievert said the mark had not yet fully corrected its levels against the currencies of its major trading parterns.
"The mark's real exchange rate against our chief trading partners rose strongly in 1994 and 1995, an incorrect development which has eased significantly this year, but not fully," he said.

Foreign exchange turbulences over the 1980s and 1990s and a strong appreciation of the German mark had probably contributed to an unusually stubborn phase of economic stagnation in Germany, from which the country had only started to escape in the second quarter of this year, he added.

"Improving the way the labour market functions, making it easier to correct market imbalances, that seems to me the most important expectation that one can pin on monetary union," he said. "There will be no more currency fluctuations to make jobs, or investment in jobs, unpredictably uncompetitive and thus, unprofitable."
